task: Create the file solution.py implementing merge_intervals(intervals) exactly as specified in the context.
context:
Module: solution.py

Signature
------------
def merge_intervals(intervals: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int]]

Behavior
------------
- intervals is a list of (start, end) pairs of ints given in arbitrary order. start <= end is expected.
- Validate every interval first: if any interval has start > end, raise ValueError. Validation happens before any merging, nothing is returned in that case. The exception message text is not checked.
- Return a new list of (start, end) tuples, sorted by start ascending.
- Intervals that overlap OR touch are merged into a single interval. Touching means the end of one equals the start of the other, e.g. (1, 3) and (3, 5) merge into (1, 5).
- Two intervals merge when the start of the later one (in sorted order) is <= the end of the current merged interval.
- The end of a merged interval is the maximum of the ends of the merged parts, so a contained interval such as (2, 5) inside (1, 10) leaves the result (1, 10).
- Duplicate intervals collapse into one interval.
- Zero-length intervals (start == end) are allowed and touch on both sides, so (5, 5) and (5, 7) merge into (5, 7).
- Bounds may be negative.
- Empty input returns [].
- Single-interval input returns a list containing exactly one tuple, e.g. [(2, 5)].
- Every returned interval must be a tuple, not a list.
- The input list must not be mutated.
- No printing and no import-time side effects; the module must define merge_intervals at module level and be importable as `from solution import merge_intervals`.

Examples
------------
merge_intervals([]) -> []
merge_intervals([(2, 5)]) -> [(2, 5)]
merge_intervals([(1, 3), (3, 5)]) -> [(1, 5)]
merge_intervals([(10, 12), (1, 3), (5, 7)]) -> [(1, 3), (5, 7), (10, 12)]
merge_intervals([(1, 10), (2, 5)]) -> [(1, 10)]
merge_intervals([(5, 4)]) -> ValueError
